nameStory: The name 'Ceratinops crenatus' comes from Greek roots meaning 'horn-like face' with 'crenatus' referring to the scalloped or notched edges found on parts of the spider's body. As a member of the dwarf weavers, this tiny spider lives up to its family's reputation for being among the smallest web-builders you'll encounter. The 'sheetweb' part of the family name describes the flat, platform-like webs these spiders construct.
description: Ceratinops crenatus is a tiny dwarf spider that belongs to the sheetweb weaver family, making it one of the smallest web-building spiders in New England. Like other dwarf spiders, it has a compact, rounded body that's typically less than 2-3 millimeters long - about the size of a pinhead. Its coloration tends toward pale browns and yellows, helping it blend seamlessly into leaf litter and low vegetation. Despite its diminutive size, this spider is a skilled web architect, creating delicate sheet webs to capture even tinier prey.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small at just 2-3mm long, roughly the size of a large pinhead - you'll need a magnifying glass or close-up phone camera to see details clearly

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds tiny horizontal sheet webs close to the ground, feeling like delicate tissue paper if accidentally brushed with a finger

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and rounded with a globular abdomen, appearing almost bead-like when viewed from above

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Pale brown to yellowish coloration with subtle darker patterns that can only be seen clearly under magnification

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves slowly and deliberately through leaf litter, often remaining motionless when disturbed rather than running away

habitat: Look for this tiny spider in moist leaf litter, low-growing vegetation, and moss in forested areas throughout New England. It prefers humid microhabitats near the ground where its minute sheet webs can capture small insects and springtails. You're most likely to encounter it when carefully examining debris piles or turning over logs in deciduous or mixed woodlands.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to build their tiny sheet webs in emerging vegetation and fresh leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most easily found, actively hunting and maintaining webs in the humid understory.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and egg sacs are produced before adults begin seeking protected overwintering sites in deep leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive, sheltering deep in leaf litter, under bark, or in other protected microhabitats until spring warmth returns.

funFact: This spider is so rare in New England that it has only been officially documented once in the entire region - making any sighting a potentially significant scientific discovery worth reporting to local naturalist groups!
confusionNotes: With only one confirmed New England observation, this species is easily confused with other tiny dwarf spiders in the same family, all of which require microscopic examination of reproductive structures for definitive identification. The key distinguishing feature is the 'crenated' or notched body structures, but these details are only visible under high magnification.
contextualKnowledge: The extremely low observation count (just 1) in New England suggests this species may be either genuinely rare in the region, under-surveyed due to its tiny size, or possibly misidentified in past collections. Many dwarf spider species require expert examination to distinguish from one another.
compareHints: Ceratinops crenatus is distinguished from its close relative C. rugosus by the crenated (notched) versus rugose (wrinkled) surface textures on specific body parts, though these differences require microscopic examination. Both species share the same tiny size and general body plan, making field identification between them virtually impossible without laboratory analysis.
